narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the 2nd decile is noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were admitted, signaling weaker recent academic performance in law school. This was the dominant reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 3.00 it is modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students and worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to offset the other factors.

Your family income bracket (upper-middle) ranked third. It also nudged the prediction toward failure, though the effect was smaller. Among accepted students, upper-middle income is actually the most common category, so this feature reflected a typical rather than unusual background.

In short, your recent law-school grades were the main obstacle. To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance in the remaining years, seek targeted bar-prep support, and consider reapplying once you have a clearer record of improvement.
